#Part A - Creating Data Frames

#Question #1
Create a data frame
```{r}
survey <- data.frame(
  Respondents        = 1:20,
  Sex                = c(2,2,1,2,2,2,2,2,2,2,1,2,2,2,2,2,2,2,1,2),
  Fathers_Occupation = c(1,3,3,3,1,2,3,1,1,1,3,2,1,3,3,1,3,1,2,1),
  Persons_at_Home    = c(5,7,3,8,5,9,6,7,8,4,7,5,4,7,8,8,3,11,7,6),
  Siblings_at_School = c(6,4,4,1,2,1,5,3,1,2,3,2,5,5,2,1,2,5,3,2),
  Types_of_Houses    = c(1,2,3,1,1,3,3,1,2,3,2,3,2,2,3,3,3,3,3,2)
)
survey
```

Subset it
```{r}
survey[survey$Sex == 1, ]           
survey[survey$Persons_at_Home > 6, ]      
survey[, c("Sex", "Types_of_Houses")]     
```

Inspect its properties
```{r}
str(survey)
dim(survey)
names(survey)
summary(survey)
head(survey)
```

Recode it
```{r}
survey$Sex <- factor(survey$Sex, levels = 1:2,
                     labels = c("Male", "Female"))
survey$Fathers_Occupation <- factor(survey$Fathers_Occupation, levels = 1:3,
                                    labels = c("Farmer", "Driver", "Others"))
survey$Types_of_Houses <- factor(survey$Types_of_Houses, levels = 1:3,
                                 labels = c("Wood", "Semi-Concrete", "Concrete"))
str(survey)
```
Analyze it
```{r}
table(survey$Sex)
table(survey$Fathers_Occupation)
table(survey$Types_of_Houses)
table(survey$Sex, survey$Types_of_Houses)  
mean(survey$Persons_at_Home)
mean(survey$Siblings_at_School)
tapply(survey$Persons_at_Home, survey$Types_of_Houses, mean)
```

length(Respondent)

#Question #2
Each row represents one respondent, so every column must have exactly 20 values for the answers to line up with the right person. If one vector were shorter or longer, data.frame() would either error or mismatch answers across respondents, making the data unreliable.

#Question #3
Sex, FathersOccupation, and TypesOfHouses are nominal data, where the numbers are just labels for categories. PersonsAtHome and SiblingsAtSchool are actual counts. Averaging Sex would be misleading because a result like 1.85 has no real meaning, and it would change if the codes were swapped even though the people are the same.



#Question #4
```{r}
survey[survey$Sex == 1, ]
```
Someone unfamiliar with the legend would see only 1s in the Sex column and have no idea whether 1 means male, female, or something else, and the other coded columns would be just as unreadable. This shows that coded data is meaningless without its legend, so it should be converted to labeled factors before sharing or interpreting results.

#Question #5
```{r}
nrow(survey[survey$Sex == 1, ])
sum(survey$Sex == 1)
```
Both give 3, so only 3 of the 20 respondents are male. This small sample (and its lopsided split of 3 males to 17 females) makes me much less confident about generalizing any pattern to a larger population, because a few respondents can swing the results and the sample may not represent the population.

Note: run these before converting Sex into a factor. If you’ve already done part c, Sex == 1 won’t match anything, so use Sex == "Male" instead.

#Question #6
```{r}
summary(survey)
```
R doesn’t know Sex and TypesOfHouses are categories because they are stored as plain numbers, and R treats any numeric column as a quantity unless you tell it otherwise (for example with factor()). This shows that how data is stored (1, 2, 3) is separate from what it means (Male/Female, Wood/Semi-Concrete/Concrete), so the meaning has to be supplied by the analyst.

#Question #7
```{r}
mean(survey$PersonsAtHome)
mean(survey$Sex)
```
The mean of PersonsAtHome (about 6.5) is meaningful because it is a real count, so it tells you the average household size in the sample. The mean of Sex (1.85) is not meaningful because 1 and 2 are only labels, so the result doesn’t describe any person or group and would change if the codes were swapped.
